articles.body: Слишком добрый ИИ-судья: измеряем ложные успехи компьютерного агента | The Overly Generous AI Judge — Agent Lab Journal Agent Lab Journal Guides Glossary Слишком добрый ИИ-судья: измеряем ложные успехи компьютерного агента The overly generous AI judge: measuring false successes of a computer-use agent Level: advanced · Reading time: 50 minutes · Updated: 10 October 2026 Your computer-use agent reports 70% task success. The number came from a model judge that looked at the final screenshot and said "yes". Now open the actual file system, the actual database, the actual settings file — and count again. If the second number is lower, the gap is made of false positives: unfinished tasks that the judge happily accepted. That gap does not just flatter a dashboard.

articles.title: I Built EcoBingo to Make Touching Grass a Little More Fun
articles.excerpt: I Built EcoBingo to Make Touching Grass More Fun This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass I wanted to build something that gives people a reason to put t…
articles.body: I Built EcoBingo to Make Touching Grass More Fun This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built I wanted to build something that gives people a reason to put their phones down and spend a little more time outside. That's how I came up with EcoBingo . It's an outdoor activity game built around a bingo board of small missions. Complete activities, earn points, build streaks, and take on weekly challenges. I also added an AI Eco Coach. Tell it what you're interested in or how much time you have, and it'll generate three personalized outdoor or eco-friendly missions for you. The goal is to make getting outside feel less like another task on your to-do list and more like something you actually want to do.

articles.title: Rate Limiting for Promo Campaigns: Keeping Flash Sales Alive Under Load
articles.excerpt: Promo drops are the sharpest traffic spike a digital storefront will ever see. A campaign that converts a few hundred checkouts a day can suddenly face tens of thousands of requests in the first minut…
articles.body: Promo drops are the sharpest traffic spike a digital storefront will ever see. A campaign that converts a few hundred checkouts a day can suddenly face tens of thousands of requests in the first minute after a code goes live. If your rate limiting was designed for average traffic, the promotion itself becomes a self-inflicted DDoS: legitimate buyers get errors, bots hoard inventory, and the campaign ends in a support inbox full of complaints. At Kadokey , where promo campaigns run regularly across digital gift cards and top-ups, we treat rate limiting as campaign infrastructure, not an afterthought. Here is the model we use. Why promo traffic is different Normal traffic grows gradually. Promo traffic does not: Thundering herd.

articles.title: I checked 2,905 npm packages with 1M+ weekly downloads. 887 haven't shipped a release in over a year.
articles.excerpt: I run a one-person software studio. Last week I built a dated index of "stale but critical" npm packages. This post is the walkthrough: the method, the numbers, what surprised me, and the caveats that…
articles.body: I run a one-person software studio. Last week I built a dated index of "stale but critical" npm packages. This post is the walkthrough: the method, the numbers, what surprised me, and the caveats that keep the headline honest. npm packages don't expire. A package published once in 2015 with a loud deprecation notice keeps flowing into npm install for as long as other packages depend on it. Weekly download counts tell you a package is alive in the ecosystem; they say nothing about whether anyone has shipped anything for it lately. So I asked the boring version of the supply-chain question: of the packages the JavaScript world downloads the most, how many haven't published a release in a year or more?

articles.excerpt: Smart assist would clean up your messy speech before translating.
articles.body: TL;DR Google introduced Rambler for Gboard earlier this year, removing filler words and cleaning up your voice input for text conversion. Now Google Translate appears to be preparing its own similar mode called Smart assist. It’s not yet clear if Smart assist would have some of the same limitations as Rambler. Voice-to-text sounds like a great idea… until you actually listen closely to how people really speak. While we expect the written word to be clear and formal, speech is often anything but — and that’s exactly why we have tools like Rambler in Gboard , able to compensate for our messy utterances.
